_about: Mock 2 (Problem Solving only): the 25 past TSA Problem Solving questions judged hardest of all those not in Mock 1, whatever their type. Shortlist from the Mock 1 judging (each earlier judge's estimates shifted to match the later judges), then two fresh judges scored every shortlisted question on one scale; score = mean of the two judges and the earlier estimate. Questions with a debatable official answer are left out. rank = 1 for the hardest of the 25.

PS.why: You have to count how many bars each floor number uses in this particular display style, which differs from the usual one for some digits. Then you must be careful about which floors are actually possible.
The big shapes in the patterns are distracting: the unusual-looking ones are not necessarily the impossible ones. You need to check what each individual tile would have to look like.
Working out the full price per person is quick, but it is easy to forget to check whether the second shop qualifies for the discount, and the options are set up to catch exactly that.

Four of the five views are genuine, and the impossible one differs from a real view only by being a mirror image, so you have to track which way round the end triangles and long faces sit once the card is folded.

The obvious reading of the first change leads to a contradiction, and you only escape it by noticing what the other digits tell you about the real times. Then you must sort out which bars are stuck on and which are stuck off.

All five nets share one layout and differ only in which small triangles are shaded, so you must work out exactly which edge each shaded triangle touches after folding, and which way round the corner reads. One misplaced triangle leads you to a near-identical wrong net.
You have to rebuild a 3D stack from an isometric drawing, including cubes you cannot see, and then picture it from an unusual direction; the mirror image of the true view is among the options.

Every view has to be checked both for which letters can sit together and for how each letter is turned, and two views show the same three faces with one letter turned differently. Tracking letter orientation on the top face after folding is where most people slip.
You must work out which digits such dates can use, then combine the two age clues. It is a long logical chain, though testing the options can shorten it.
Spotting which faces are opposite each other rules out several cubes, but the last two candidates differ only in the direction of a diagonal stripe, which needs careful folding.
A natural shortcut with the 12% answers a slightly different question; you must be careful about whose laps you are counting and about counting completed laps rather than rounding.

Each view shows three faces meeting at a corner, and the impossible one has a valid set of three colours in the wrong clockwise order; the corner formed by the three outer flaps is the hardest to picture.
Some candidate tiles are mirror images of each other. Floor tiles can be turned but not flipped over, so you must check each one against the floor carefully.

Either player can use either symbol, so any line you set up can be completed by your opponent first. You have to see what kind of position actually forces a win and check every reply the opponent could make.
Several pieces have the right area and look as if they ought to fit. Seeing how four copies actually fill the trapezium needs a dissection idea that is not obvious.

Every option passes the usual opposite-faces and corner-order checks, so you have to notice a much subtler feature of how the spots are laid out. Most people run out of ideas (or time) before spotting it.

You must translate the walking clues into a fact about the shape of the path network, especially which junctions every route has to go through. Then you must be strict about which landmarks are genuinely pinned down.
The minimum spend comes from a lower bound plus a cutting plan that actually achieves it. The plan is fiddly to find, so many people stop at the first workable answer, which is not the cheapest.

The same face can look different when it is seen at an angle, so you first have to work out which symbols are really the same face. Only then can you pin down the opposite pairs and which way each symbol points.

There are 35 blocks to sort by size and the pie charts have no key, so you must match the three proportions by angle alone; one wrong chart is very close to the right one, so a single miscount misleads you.
Octahedron nets are unfamiliar and are drawn here at an awkward slant. Some options can be ruled out quickly, but separating the last few needs careful mental folding.
Both the evening and the morning views were reflections, so the watch was set wrong by a definite amount; you then have to reverse the order of the digits and flip each one, which is easy to muddle.

Two nets put the letters in the same places and differ only in how the letters are turned, so getting the neighbours right is not enough: you must also check how the letters on the top face are rotated in both views.
Counting tiles in the drawing gives a misleading ratio because of the cut-off edges; you need to find the repeating unit around one hexagon and count only the triangles that belong to it.
The trap is to slide one hole across onto the other; when the sheet is folded one hole is flipped over, and that changes which pair of shapes gives the octagon.
